QF.id: AIFM AIFs in India and Suitability_5

question.text: Ms. Meera Subramanian, aged 42, has an INR 100 crore portfolio currently invested 25% Large-cap, 25% Small-cap, 20% Unlisted, 15% Listed Corporate Debt, 10% G-Secs, 5% Money Market. She has capped her exposure to any single asset class at 40%. She wishes to re-allocate the 20% Unlisted allocation (INR 20 crore) into Category III AIFs, choosing between Fund A (long-short, Mid-cap only) and Fund B (market-neutral, 80% Small-cap and 20% Mid-cap). As her fund manager, which re-allocation is MOST consistent with her concentration policy?

answer.text: Allocate the entire INR 20 crore to Fund B for diversification benefits
Split INR 10 crore each to Fund A and Fund B
Allocate the entire INR 20 crore to Fund A
Retain the allocation in domestic unlisted securities since any Cat III allocation will breach her cap

explanation.text: The Logic: Existing Small-cap exposure is already 25% of the INR 100 crore portfolio. Allocating the entire INR 20 crore to Fund B would inject 80% x INR 20 crore = INR 16 crore (16% of the portfolio) of additional Small-cap, pushing Small-cap to 25% + 16% = 41% and breaching the 40% concentration cap. Fund A (Mid-cap only) does not add to Small-cap exposure, so the full INR 20 crore can go to Fund A without breaching the cap — matching the worked example in the chapter. The Trap: Option A looks diversified but mechanically breaches the 40% Small-cap cap. Option B still adds about 8% Small-cap on top of the existing 25%, which stays under the cap but is inferior to a fully compliant allocation. Option D ignores that the investor has already decided to re-allocate away from unlisted. Note: Look-through analysis of an AIF's underlying asset-class exposures is the key step here — the cap binds at the portfolio level, not at the fund-selection level.
